extracted.intended_audience: federal trial judges, litigators, and jurors in U.S. patent litigation (users of model jury instructions)
extracted.subtask_description: Model patent jury instructions for federal patent trials providing legal standards, definitions, and jury guidance on claim construction, infringement, invalidity, damages (including FRAND and apportionment), and related issues. Intended to be adapted by judges for use in trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: WHAT A PATENT IS AND HOW ONE IS OBTAINED
rubrics_metrics.description: Explains what a patent is, its parts (specification, drawings, claims), term, and the PTO examination/prosecution process by which patents are granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides background information jurors must understand; defines patent as exclusive right granted by the U.S. PTO, typical 20-year term, and that patents are issued after examination of an application that includes specification, drawings and claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: SUMMARY OF CONTENTIONS
rubrics_metrics.description: A plain-language summary of the parties’ positions on liability and damages for the jury’s orientation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used at the start of trial to outline what each party contends; not evidentiary, but frames issues jurors will decide.

rubrics_metrics.name: PATENT AT ISSUE
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the asserted patent(s) and the claims at issue in the case for the jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains which patent(s) and which claim(s) the jury must consider; may include brief background of the patented technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: OVERVIEW OF APPLICABLE LAW
rubrics_metrics.description: High-level statement of the legal framework governing patent validity, infringement, and damages the jury must apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarizes relevant legal standards the jury will receive in more detail in subsequent instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: OUTLINE OF TRIAL
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanation of trial phases, what evidence will be presented, and the jury’s role during trial and deliberations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes sequence (opening statements, evidence, expert testimony, closing arguments, instructions, deliberation), and practical notes for jurors (e.g., taking notes, not discussing case outside deliberations).

rubrics_metrics.name: PATENT CLAIMS (Claim Construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe what patent claims are (concise, formal definitions that set the boundaries of the invention) and how they should be read for infringement/validity analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that each claim is a numbered paragraph, may be independent or dependent, and that infringement requires that an accused device or method contain every claim limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: INDEPENDENT AND DEPENDENT CLAIMS
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes independent claims (stand alone) from dependent claims (refer to and incorporate other claims) and how jurors should treat them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that dependent claims incorporate the limitations of the referenced claim(s) and stand only if the claim they depend upon is valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: SECTION 112, PARAGRAPH 6 / 35 U.S.C. § 112(f) (means-plus-function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction on claims that use means-plus-function language and how such claim elements are construed and infringed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that certain claim language may be interpreted to cover the corresponding structure, materials, or acts described in the specification and equivalents; sets standard for reading such limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: INFRINGEMENT GENERALLY
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal standard for what constitutes infringement (making, using, selling, offering to sell, or importing a patented invention within the United States during the patent term without permission).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains direct, indirect (inducement and contributory), and other forms of infringement; jury must determine whether the accused product or action meets each claim limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: DIRECT INFRINGEMENT — LITERAL INFRINGEMENT
rubrics_metrics.description: A device or method literally infringes if it contains each and every limitation of the asserted claim exactly as claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors must compare accused products/methods to the claim language element-by-element; if every limitation is present as claimed, literal infringement exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: DIRECT INFRINGEMENT — LITERAL INFRINGEMENT OF §112(f) (means-plus-function) LIMITATIONS
rubrics_metrics.description: How literal infringement analysis applies when claim limitations are expressed in means-plus-function form under §112(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires comparing accused structure/acts to the corresponding structure/materials/acts disclosed in the specification (and equivalents) that perform the claimed function.

rubrics_metrics.name: DIRECT INFRINGEMENT — DOCTRINE OF EQUIVALENTS
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if an accused product/method does not literally meet every limitation, it may infringe under the doctrine of equivalents if differences are insubstantial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides the framework jurors should use to assess equivalence (e.g., function-way-result or other applicable tests); also notes limits and defenses to DOE (some limitations/restrictions discussed and some sections deleted in model).

rubrics_metrics.name: INDIRECT INFRINGEMENT — ACTIVE INDUCEMENT
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements the plaintiff must prove to show inducement to infringe (intent and evidence of acts that encourage or aid another to directly infringe).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors must find that the accused inducer knew of the patent, knew its actions would induce infringement, and took active steps to encourage direct infringement; includes intent-related analysis and relevant evidence standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: INDIRECT INFRINGEMENT — CONTRIBUTORY INFRINGEMENT
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirements for contributory infringement (offering to sell or selling a component especially made for use in an infringing product, knowing it is especially made for infringement and not a staple article of commerce).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains knowledge and design-for-infringement requirements, and that common items suitable for substantial noninfringing uses are typically not contributory infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: INFRINGEMENT THROUGH SUPPLY OF COMPONENTS FROM U.S. FOR COMBINATION ABROAD
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructions on infringement liability for supplying components from the United States that are combined abroad in an infringing manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains when supplying components for overseas combination can give rise to liability under U.S. patent law (including statutory and case-law constraints).

rubrics_metrics.name: INFRINGEMENT BY SALE, OFFER FOR SALE, USE, OR IMPORTATION OF PRODUCT MADE OUTSIDE U.S. BY PATENTED PROCESS
rubrics_metrics.description: How infringement is treated when a product made abroad by a patented process is sold, offered, used, or imported into the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains statutory rules and case law that determine when such acts constitute infringement of a U.S. patent on a process.

rubrics_metrics.name: DIRECT INFRINGEMENT: SYSTEMS WITH COMPONENTS OUTSIDE THE UNITED STATES
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction on when a system with one or more components located outside the U.S. can or cannot constitute direct infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers the requirement that all acts making up direct infringement occur within the U.S.; explains combining acts across borders and relevant precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: DIRECT INFRINGEMENT: MULTIPLE PARTIES' ACTS MUST BE COMBINED FOR METHOD CLAIMS
rubrics_metrics.description: When asserted method claims require multiple parties to perform different steps, jury must consider whether one actor is liable for combined acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains legal tests for attributing steps performed by different parties to a single actor (joint enterprise, direction/control, agency), and when combination can satisfy all claim steps for infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: WILLFUL INFRINGEMENT
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard for finding willful infringement and implications (e.g., potential enhanced damages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes factors jurors may consider (defendant’s knowledge of the patent, objective reasonableness of noninfringement/invalidity positions) and references Halo (Supreme Court) guidance; typically a fact-specific inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: INVALIDITY — BURDEN OF PROOF
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff must prove infringement, while the defendant challenging validity bears the burden to prove invalidity by the applicable standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States the burden and standard (e.g., clear and convincing evidence for patent invalidity in civil cases) and any nuances depending on precedent and circumstance.

rubrics_metrics.name: WRITTEN DESCRIPTION REQUIREMENT (§112)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must contain a written description sufficient to show that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention at the time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains what written description means, what jurors should look for in the specification, and consequences of failing the requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: ENABLEMENT (§112)
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent specification must enable persons skilled in the art to make and use the invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors should consider whether the disclosure provides sufficient detail and guidance for a skilled person to practice the invention across the full scope of the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: BEST MODE (deleted placeholder)
rubrics_metrics.description: (Model document marks instruction as deleted) Historically, patentees had to disclose the best mode. The model includes a deleted note for jurisdictions/times where best mode is not applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction omitted/deleted in model where not applicable; judges tailor for cases where best mode remains relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: PRIOR ART — IDENTIFYING RELEVANT REFERENCES
rubrics_metrics.description: How to determine what constitutes prior art for anticipation and obviousness analyses, including relevant timeframes (pre-AIA vs post-AIA rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains which publications, patents, uses, sales, or other disclosures count as prior art under the patent statutes and controlling case law; differentiates effective filing date rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: ANTICIPATION
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is invalid as anticipated if a single prior-art reference discloses each and every claim limitation (i.e., the claimed invention is not new).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors must determine whether a single prior reference reads on all claim elements; requires clear and convincing proof if challenging validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: OBVIOUSNESS
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim invalidity for obviousness requires showing that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art at the relevant time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes subfactors jurors should consider (level of ordinary skill, scope and content of prior art, differences between prior art and claims, objective indicia of nonobviousness). References Graham factors and controlling precedent (e.g., KSR).

rubrics_metrics.name: LEVEL OF ORDINARY SKILL IN THE ART
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact-specific determination of the qualifications and knowledge of a hypothetical person of ordinary skill relevant to obviousness analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors should consider education, experience, types of problems encountered in the art, and analogous evidence when assessing obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: SCOPE AND CONTENT OF THE PRIOR ART
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify what the relevant prior art discloses and whether it is analogous to the claimed invention for obviousness purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors should evaluate the teachings of prior references and whether they are properly combinable under the law to render claims obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: INVENTORSHIP
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination of who qualifies as an inventor and whether inventorship is correct for patent validity/ownership issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains legal tests for inventorship (conception and reduction to practice), and that incorrect inventorship may affect patent validity or ownership rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: DAMAGES — INTRODUCTION
rubrics_metrics.description: General instructions on the jury’s role in awarding damages for patent infringement and types of damages available (lost profits, reasonable royalty, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains purposes of damages (compensation for past infringement), available forms of relief, and burden of proof for damages claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: LOST PROFITS — 'BUT FOR' TEST
rubrics_metrics.description: Framework for awarding lost profits: plaintiff must show sales would have occurred 'but for' the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model discusses Panduit and related tests and evidence categories; jurors consider causation, demand, absence of acceptable noninfringing substitutes, capacity, and measure of profit.

rubrics_metrics.name: LOST PROFITS — DEMAND
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff must prove demand for the patented product or its features to recover lost profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors assess whether customers wanted the patented feature/product and whether demand existed independent of infringer’s actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: LOST PROFITS — NONINFRINGING SUBSTITUTES — ACCEPTABILITY
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether acceptable noninfringing substitutes existed that customers would have used instead of the patented product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether substitutes were acceptable to customers in the relevant market and would have been used in the absence of infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: LOST PROFITS — NONINFRINGING SUBSTITUTES — AVAILABILITY
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether acceptable noninfringing substitutes were available in the relevant time period to meet demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors evaluate whether substitutes were practically available to replace the patented product during the damages period.

rubrics_metrics.name: LOST PROFITS — CAPACITY
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the plaintiff had the capacity to meet demand and therefore could have made the lost sales 'but for' infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider plaintiff’s production capabilities, reasonably probable expansion, and other capacity-related evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: LOST PROFITS — AMOUNT OF PROFIT
rubrics_metrics.description: How to calculate the amount of profit the plaintiff lost as a result of the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes instructions on measuring profit (e.g., using accounting records, allocating profit margins) and distinguishing between profit and other measures of damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: LOST PROFITS — MARKET SHARE
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of market share evidence to calculate lost profits where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains when market share methods are reasonable and how jurors should apply market share to measure lost profits.

rubrics_metrics.name: LOST PROFITS — COLLATERAL SALES
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of lost profits on collateral sales that accompany the patented product (e.g., consumables, accessories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors evaluate whether collateral sales were causally linked to the patented product and should be included in lost profit calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: LOST PROFITS — PRICE EROSION
rubrics_metrics.description: Compensation for reduction in plaintiff’s prices caused by defendant’s infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains when price erosion evidence is relevant and how jurors may calculate damages for price erosion.

rubrics_metrics.name: REASONABLE ROYALTY — ENTITLEMENT
rubrics_metrics.description: When a plaintiff who cannot prove lost profits may still recover a reasonable royalty as compensation for infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors must decide whether a reasonable royalty is warranted and then compute an appropriate royalty based on the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: REASONABLE ROYALTY — DEFINITION
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable royalty is the amount a willing licensor and willing licensee would have agreed upon at the time infringement began.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides hypothetical negotiation framework (Georgia-Pacific factors and other considerations) jurors may use to determine royalty rate and base.

rubrics_metrics.name: DAMAGES — LUMP SUM VS. RUNNING ROYALTY
rubrics_metrics.description: Options for structuring a royalty award as a one-time lump sum or as a running (ongoing) royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains differences and factors relevant to choosing between lump-sum and running royalties, depending on facts and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: REASONABLE ROYALTY — RELEVANT FACTORS (e.g., Georgia‑Pacific)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors jurors may consider in assessing a reasonable royalty, such as royalties from comparable licenses, profitability, and the nature of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model identifies typical Georgia‑Pacific factors and instructs jurors to weigh all relevant evidence presented to reach a reasonable royalty determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: DAMAGES — COMPARABLE AGREEMENTS
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of comparable licensing agreements as evidence to inform a reasonable royalty award.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors should assess relevance and comparability of licensing agreements (e.g., similarity of technologies, parties, negotiation circumstances) and may accept or reject specific figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: DATE OF COMMENCEMENT OF DAMAGES — PRODUCTS
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction on when damages begin for products (notice/marking rules and statutory constraints).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains marking and notice requirements (35 U.S.C. §287) and that method claims may have different rules; provides examples where damage period begins at issuance or at first infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: DAMAGES — FAIR, REASONABLE, AND NON‑DISCRIMINATORY (FRAND) TERMS FOR SEPS
rubrics_metrics.description: When the asserted patent is alleged to be standard-essential, jurors must ensure royalties reflect that the patentee declared the patent essential and agreed to license on FRAND terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patent is essential to a standard, jurors must apportion royalty from value of the standard as a whole and base the royalty on the value of the invention, not value added by standardization; non-discrimination means similarly situated firms should receive similar terms. Jurors may consider evidence of patent hold-up and royalty stacking if presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: DAMAGES — APPORTIONMENT
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasonable royalty (and typically lost profits) awards must be apportioned to reflect only the value attributable to the patented invention, not unpatented features or other factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains apportionment concept, the narrow 'entire market value rule' exception (requires patented feature to be sole driver of customer demand), and that apportionment requires separating value of patented features from other features, marketing, or market position. Notes that apportionment instruction tailoring may be necessary depending on facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: GLOSSARY — KEY TERMS (Abstract, Claim, Enablement, Anticipation, Prior Art, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions of patent-law terms jurors will encounter (e.g., abstract, claim, limitation, enablement, anticipation, prior art, prosecution history, reads on).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These definitions control deliberations where the instructions define terms; judges should add technical terms from the case’s art and delete inapplicable terms.
